title: Net Worth: What It Is and How to Work Out Yours
description: How to calculate your net worth in four steps, why a negative number is normal in your 20s, and how it moves month by month. Free tracker included.
keywords: how to calculate net worth what is net worth net worth calculator negative net worth net worth in your 20s
takeaways: Net worth is what you own minus what you owe.
A negative number is normal when you have student loans and few savings.
Check it every few months. The direction matters more than the number.
body:
Most net worth guides open with a house worth $300,000 and a fat investment portfolio. If you rent a room, have a few hundred dollars in the bank and a student loan following you around, those examples feel like they were written for someone else. They were, in a way. This one is written for you. Your net worth is a single number: everything you own, minus everything you owe. Learning how to calculate net worth takes about ten minutes with your banking app open, and you do not need a house, investments or a high salary to do it. By the end of this page you will have your number, you will know how much its size actually matters (less than you think), and you will know how to watch it move in the right direction. ## What net worth actually means The formula fits on one line: Net worth = what you own (your assets) - what you owe (your liabilities) The Student Money Management Center at the University of Illinois describes the same calculation: add up the value of all your assets, then subtract your liabilities, or debts, from that total. The result is a measure of where your money stands at one point in time. Two things are worth understanding before you start. First, net worth is a snapshot, not a grade. It describes today, and today only. Second, it is not the same as your income. Your salary is money flowing through your life. Your net worth is what has actually stuck. Two people can earn the exact same pay and have completely different numbers, because one kept some of it and the other carries more debt. That is why this number is worth knowing even when it is small, and even when it is below zero. ## What counts as an asset when you are in your 20s An asset is something you own that has a cash value: money you could reach, or something you could sell. At this age your list is probably short, and a short list is fine. ### Money you already have - Checking and savings account balances - Cash, including balances sitting in payment apps - A workplace retirement account, such as a 401(k), even if the balance is tiny - Any investments, such as a small brokerage account or a few shares ### Bigger things you own Your car is the main one for most people in their 20s. Count it at what you could realistically sell it for today, not what you paid for it. Cars lose value fast, and using the old purchase price just flatters the number. If you own anything else with a genuine resale value, such as a musical instrument or camera gear you could sell this week at a price you can check online, you can include it at that honest resale price. ### What to leave out Your wardrobe does not count, even if you spent a lot on it. Neither does your phone, your furniture or the contents of your kitchen drawers. Yes, you could sell some of it, but the resale money is so small compared with the effort of valuing it that most people who track net worth leave everyday belongings out. Leave out your degree, too. It may well raise your earnings later, but you cannot sell it, so it is not an asset in this calculation. Future pay never counts. Only what exists today counts. One grey area: the deposit your landlord holds. That money should come back to you, so some people count it. Most leave it off to keep things simple. Either way is fine, as long as you treat it the same way every time you redo the sums. ## What counts as a liability A liability is any balance you owe to someone else. Use the balance as it stands today, not the amount you originally borrowed and not the monthly payment. - Student loan balance, even if your payments are currently paused - Credit card balances - A car loan, if you have one - Personal loans and any buy now, pay later balances - An overdraft, and money borrowed from family that you genuinely plan to repay If you are not sure what you owe, open each app or statement and write down the real figure. Guessing low feels better for a minute and teaches you nothing. ## How to calculate net worth in four steps 1. List everything you own from the asset categories above, with today's value next to each item. 2. Add the values up. That total is your assets. 3. List everything you owe, with today's balance next to each debt. Add those up too. That total is your liabilities. 4. Subtract the second total from the first. Whatever is left, positive or negative, is your net worth. Write the date next to your number. A net worth figure without a date is not much use, because the whole point is comparing it with the same figure later. ## A worked example: a renter at 23 Here is the full calculation for an imaginary 23-year-old renter. The numbers are made up to show how the maths works, and they are deliberately small, because small is where most people start. | What she owns (assets) | Value | |-------------------------------|----------| | Checking account | $320 | | Savings account | $480 | | Car, at today's resale value | $2,000 | | Total assets | $2,800 | | What she owes (liabilities) | Balance | | Student loan | $6,000 | | Credit card balance | $450 | | Total liabilities | $6,450 | | Net worth ($2,800 - $6,450) | -$3,650 | No house. No portfolio. A bank balance of $800, a $2,000 car, a $6,000 student loan, and a net worth of minus $3,650. If your first attempt at this looks similar, nothing has gone wrong. You have just measured your starting point. If you would rather not do the adding on paper, a simple spreadsheet keeps each month's figure in one place and does the sums for you.

Download the free Net Worth Tracker (.xlsx)

It works in Google Sheets and Excel. No sign-up needed. ![The net worth snapshot listing what you own, what you owe and a negative net worth](/assets/img/posts/net-worth-tracker-preview-880x624.webp) ## Negative at 23 is normal It is easy to assume a negative number means you are failing. The data says otherwise. According to the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, published in October 2026, the median net worth of US families headed by someone under 35 was $33,000. Median means the middle: half of those families had less. And that figure covers whole households, including couples in their early 30s and people who already own homes. A single renter at 23 sits in a very different spot from that group. There is also a simple reason so many young people land below zero. A student loan arrives in full on day one, but the thing it paid for, your education, cannot be listed as an asset. As the University of Illinois guide points out, people with student loans and limited savings often end up with a negative net worth for exactly this reason. The loan is real and the qualification is real; only one of them fits on this list. Negative now says nothing about where you end up. It says you started, like most people, with a debt and not much else. ## How the number moves from month to month Net worth rarely jumps. It creeps. Watch what happens to our renter over six months. She saves $150 a month, makes her regular student loan payments, and clears the credit card. Her car, like every car, quietly loses a bit of value. | | January | July | |----------------------|----------|----------| | Money in the bank | $800 | $1,700 | | Car, at resale value | $2,000 | $1,850 | | Total assets | $2,800 | $3,550 | | Student loan | $6,000 | $5,520 | | Credit card | $450 | $0 | | Total owed | $6,450 | $5,520 | | Net worth | -$3,650 | -$1,970 | Six months, no pay rise, no windfall, and the number improved by $1,680. Her bank balance grew by $900, her debts fell by $930, and her car lost $150. Put together: $900 plus $930 minus $150 equals $1,680 of progress. Notice what did not move the number. Shifting money from checking to savings changes nothing, because the same dollars are still yours. Paying a bill out of your account changes nothing on its own either: your cash drops and your debt drops by the same amount. What actually moves net worth is keeping part of each paycheck instead of spending it, and paying down the principal on a debt. Small, boring, repeatable. That is the whole engine. ## How often should you recheck it? Once a month is a good rhythm for a quick version: update the balances, note the new number, move on. Five minutes is plenty once the first calculation is done. If monthly feels like too much, quarterly works well too, and the University of Illinois guide suggests quarterly or annual check-ins for tracking your progress over time. What matters is using the same method on the same rough date, so each number can be compared fairly with the last one. A monthly net worth check slots neatly into a wider once-a-month money routine. Read next: [Monthly Money Review: A 20-Minute Checklist](/blog/monthly-money-review/). Avoid checking daily. Balances wobble with paydays and bill dates, and watching the number twitch will only annoy you. This is a long game measured in months and years, not days. ## Three moves that push the number up You grow net worth from both sides: build what you own, shrink what you owe. These three moves cover most of it at this stage of life. - Start a small emergency fund before anything fancy. Even a few hundred dollars set aside means the next surprise bill does not land on a credit card and drag the number backwards. Read next: [How to Build an Emergency Fund on a Low Income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/). - Aim any spare money at one debt at a time, starting with the most expensive balance. Every dollar of principal you clear is a dollar added straight to your net worth. Read next: [How to Pay Off Credit Card Debt Fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/). - Keep your savings somewhere that pays you something. A high-yield savings account will not make you rich, but your cash may as well earn a little while it sits there. Read next: [What Is a High-Yield Savings Account?](/blog/high-yield-savings-account/). It also helps to give the number a target, such as reaching zero by a set date, and a rough plan for getting there. Read next: [How to Set Financial Goals You Actually Reach](/blog/set-financial-goals/). ## Frequently asked questions ### Does my salary count as an asset? No. Income is money that flows in and out. Only what you still have from it, sitting in an account or owned outright, counts toward net worth. ### Should I include my car if I still owe money on it? Yes, both sides of it. List the car at its current resale value as an asset, and list the remaining loan balance as a liability. The gap between the two is what the car really adds or takes away. ### Will a negative net worth hurt my credit score? No. Net worth is not part of your credit score, and nobody reports it anywhere. It is a private number for your own tracking. Lenders look at your income, your debts and how you handle payments, which is related territory, but your net worth figure itself stays yours. ### My student loan payments are paused. Does the loan still count? Yes. A pause stops the payments, not the debt. The balance is still owed, so it still belongs on your list at its full current amount. ### What about money in apps like PayPal or Venmo? Count it. It is your cash, wherever it happens to sit. The same goes for gift cards only if you would genuinely count their value, though most people skip anything that small. ### Is it worth calculating if I know it will be negative? Yes, and arguably that is when it helps most. A negative first number is a starting line with a date on it. Watching it climb toward zero, month by month, is one of the clearest signs that your money habits are working. Disclaimer: This article is general education only and is not financial, tax or legal advice for your specific situation. Figures from surveys describe groups of households, not any individual. If you need advice about your own debts or taxes, talk to a qualified professional in your country. ## Sources - [Federal Reserve Board, Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025: Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances, October 2026.](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/scf26.pdf) - [University of Illinois, Student Money Management Center, Financial Feedback: Calculating Net Worth.](https://blogs.illinois.edu/view/7550/2037919254)
